stem: A company runs a media library in an Amazon S3 bucket. The bucket is the only copy of the files, and each file is larger than 10 MB. Some files are read many times each day for months. Other files are never read after their first week. Nobody can predict which files will stay popular, so the access pattern of each file is unpredictable. Which storage approach is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: the access pattern of each file is unpredictable
the only copy of the files

options.text: Store the files in S3 Standard, and add a lifecycle rule that moves every file to S3 Standard-IA 30 days after upload.
options.why: Popular files are still read after day 30, and S3 Standard-IA adds a [per-GB retrieval charge](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-standard-ia-retrieval-charge) to each of those reads.

options.text: Store the files in S3 One Zone-IA, because it costs less than S3 Standard-IA and keeps the same eleven nines of durability.
options.why: The bucket is the only copy, and S3 One Zone-IA is [not resilient to the physical loss](../facts/s3.md#s3-one-zone-ia-az-loss) of its Availability Zone.

options.text: Store the files in S3 Intelligent-Tiering, so that S3 moves each file between access tiers based on how often the file is read.
options.why: S3 Intelligent-Tiering fits [unknown, changing, or unpredictable access patterns](../facts/s3.md#s3-intelligent-tiering-ideal-for-unknown-access) and has [no retrieval fees](../facts/s3.md#s3-int-tiering-no-retrieval-fees), so reads of popular files add no retrieval charge.

options.text: Store the files in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and serve each file to users with a normal GET request when they ask for it.
options.why: A normal GET does not read this class: first you [retrieve data using the RestoreObject REST API](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-restore-needed-flexible-deep), which takes hours.

explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering [automatically stores objects in three access tiers](../facts/s3.md#s3-intelligent-tiering-automatic-tiers) and watches how often each object is read. A file that is read again is [automatically moved back to the Frequent Access tier](../facts/s3.md#s3-int-tiering-move-back), so a popular file returns to the fast tier. Objects smaller than [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-int-tiering-small-objects) are not tiered, but every file here is larger.
takeaway: An unknown or changing access pattern points to S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which charges no retrieval fee.
twin: If the stem said "every file is read about once a month" instead: S3 Standard-IA, because the pattern is known and the class suits data read [once a month](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-standard-ia-profile).
say: Nobody can predict the pattern, so I'd use Intelligent-Tiering: it moves each file for you and has no retrieval fee.

stem: A company must keep recordings of customer calls for 10 years to meet a legal rule. The recordings are audio files of 20 MB to 200 MB each, and nobody reads them during normal operations. About twice a year, auditors ask for a few recordings. A wait of up to 48 hours for those recordings is acceptable. The company wants to archive the recordings in Amazon S3. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: nobody reads them during normal operations
A wait of up to 48 hours

options.text: Store the recordings in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, and read each requested recording directly with a GET request when the auditors ask.
options.why: It works with millisecond reads, but Deep Archive is [the lowest cost storage in the cloud](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-deep-archive-lowest-cost-twelve-hours), and the stem accepts a 48-hour wait.

options.text: Store the recordings in S3 Glacier Deep Archive, and restore each requested recording with the Expedited retrieval option when the auditors ask.
options.why: From S3 Glacier Deep Archive, the Expedited retrieval option is [Not available](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-retrieval-times-deep), so this restore request fails.

options.text: Store the recordings in S3 Standard-IA, and read each requested recording directly with a GET request when the auditors ask.
options.why: It works, but the S3 Glacier classes are [most effective for rarely accessed data](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-classes-min-duration-and-retrieval-fees), and these recordings are read about twice a year.
options.misconception: picks an infrequent-access class for data that is read only twice a year

options.text: Store the recordings in S3 Glacier Deep Archive, and restore each requested recording with the Bulk retrieval option when the auditors ask.
options.why: Bulk is [the lowest-cost retrieval option](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-retrieval-options-three), and from Deep Archive it finishes [within 48 hours](../facts/s3.md#s3-retrieval-bulk-lowest-cost-48-hours-deep-archive), which the auditors accept.

explanation: The recordings are not read in normal operations, so the storage price decides. S3 Glacier Deep Archive is [the lowest cost storage in the cloud](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-deep-archive-lowest-cost-twelve-hours) for long-lived archives. An auditor request starts a restore, and the restored copy is [available only for the duration that you specify](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-restore-temporary-copy). Bulk is the cheapest restore, and its wait fits the 48 hours in the stem.
takeaway: Rarely read archive and a wait of days accepted: S3 Glacier Deep Archive with Bulk restores.
twin: If the stem said "auditors need a recording within 12 hours" instead: S3 Glacier Deep Archive with a Standard restore, because it finishes [within 12 hours](../facts/s3.md#s3-retrieval-standard-default-12-hours-deep-archive).
say: Nobody reads the calls and auditors can wait two days, so Deep Archive with a Bulk restore is cheapest.

stem: A financial services company stores trade records as objects in a new Amazon S3 bucket. An application uploads thousands of records each day. The company must retain each record in an immutable form for 7 years. Most users must not be able to delete or overwrite a record, but the security team must be able to remove the protection when a legal request requires it. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: the security team must be able to remove the protection
retain each record in an immutable form

options.text: Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket in compliance mode, and set a default retention period of 7 years that applies to every new object version.
options.why: A version in compliance mode [can't be overwritten or deleted by any user](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-compliance-mode), so the security team cannot remove the protection for a legal request.

options.text: Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket in governance mode, set a default retention period of 7 years, and allow only the security team to bypass governance retention.
options.why: Governance mode stops most users, and a user with [s3:BypassGovernanceRetention](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-governance-mode) can remove the protection, so the security team alone gets that permission.

options.text: Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket, and change the application so that every upload request sets compliance mode and a retain-until date 7 years ahead.
options.why: Every upload sets compliance mode, and a version in that mode [can't be overwritten or deleted by any user](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-compliance-mode), so the security team is locked out as well.

options.text: Turn on S3 Object Lock for the bucket, change the application so that every upload sets governance mode and a 7-year retain-until date, and let only the security team bypass it.
options.why: It works, but changing the application to set [a unique retention period for individual objects](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-retention-per-object-or-bucket-default) is more work than a bucket default.

explanation: AWS says to use governance mode when [some users with special permissions](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-mode-choice) can alter the retention or delete objects. A user who holds [s3:BypassGovernanceRetention](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-governance-mode) and sends the [x-amz-bypass-governance-retention:true](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-governance-mode) header can remove the protection. The bucket default sets [how long to protect every object version](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-bucket-default-retention), so the application needs no change.
takeaway: When a privileged team needs to remove the lock, use governance mode and give that team the bypass permission.
twin: If the stem said "No user, including the root user, can be allowed to delete or overwrite a record" instead: compliance mode, because a version [can't be overwritten or deleted by any user](../facts/s3.md#s3-object-lock-compliance-mode).
say: Governance mode stops most users, and the bypass permission lets the security team remove the lock.

stem: A company stores signed contracts as objects in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company manages its own keys in a hardware security module in its data center. Company policy says that the encryption keys must never be stored in AWS. Each object must be encrypted before it leaves the data center, so that AWS never sees unencrypted data in transit or at rest. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
keywords: keys must never be stored in AWS
encrypted before it leaves the data center

options.text: Use SSE-KMS with a customer managed key in AWS KMS, and let the company's security team control the key policy and the key rotation.
options.why: Customer managed does not mean kept by the company: the KMS key lives in AWS KMS, [in the same Region as the bucket](../facts/s3.md#s3-sse-kms-key-same-region-as-bucket).

options.text: Turn on SSE-C for the bucket, and send the company's key over HTTPS with every upload request and every download request.
options.why: With SSE-C, S3 receives the plaintext and encrypts it on arrival, so AWS sees unencrypted data, even though [S3 never stores the encryption key](../facts/s3.md#s3-sse-c-key-never-stored-https-required).

options.text: Encrypt each object in the data center with the company's key before upload, and decrypt it in the data center after download.
options.why: The objects leave the data center encrypted, so they [aren't exposed to any third party, including AWS](../facts/s3.md#s3-client-side-encryption-not-exposed-to-aws), and the company keeps its keys.

options.text: Encrypt each object in the data center before upload, and also turn on SSE-C and send the company's key with every request.
options.why: It works, because client-side encryption keeps plaintext away from AWS, but the extra SSE-C layer adds key handling on every request that the stem does not need.

explanation: The stem keeps unencrypted data away from AWS, so the encryption happens before upload. With client-side encryption, [you manage the encryption process, the encryption keys](../facts/s3.md#s3-client-side-encryption-you-manage-keys) and the tools, and S3 [does not play a role in encrypting](../facts/s3.md#s3-client-side-encryption-not-exposed-to-aws) the objects. S3 stores ciphertext, and the key stays in the hardware security module.
takeaway: Plaintext stays inside the company: encrypt client-side before upload.
twin: If the stem said "Amazon S3 must encrypt each object at rest and decrypt it" instead: SSE-C, because S3 does the work and [S3 never stores the encryption key](../facts/s3.md#s3-sse-c-key-never-stored-https-required).
say: AWS must never see the plain data, so I'd encrypt in the data center before the upload.

stem: A hospital group stores medical images in Amazon S3. Each image is between 5 MB and 50 MB, and the images must be kept for many years. Doctors open a given image about once a quarter. When a doctor opens an image, the image must load in real time, within milliseconds. The hospital group wants to reduce its storage costs. Which storage class is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: load in real time, within milliseconds

options.text: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, with an Expedited retrieval request sent each time a doctor opens one of the images.
options.why: Flexible Retrieval data is [archived, and not available for real-time access](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-classes-access-model), and an Expedited restore takes [1–5 minutes](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-retrieval-times-flexible).

options.text: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, with each image read directly by a normal GET request each time a doctor opens it.
options.why: For archive data that needs immediate access, [S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-glacier-ir-lowest-cost-milliseconds) gives the lowest storage cost with millisecond reads.

options.text: S3 Standard-IA, with each image read directly by a normal GET request each time a doctor opens one of the images.
options.why: It works with the [same latency and throughput performance](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-glacier-ir-vs-standard-ia), but Glacier Instant Retrieval stores images that are read once a quarter for less.

options.text: S3 Intelligent-Tiering with the Deep Archive Access tier turned on, with each image read by a normal GET request.
options.why: Objects in the Deep Archive Access tier need you to [first restore the object by using RestoreObject](../facts/s3.md#s3-intelligent-tiering-archive-tiers-need-restore), so a GET cannot load them in milliseconds.
options.misconception: believes that every Intelligent-Tiering tier answers a GET in milliseconds

explanation: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval suits data accessed about [once a quarter](../facts/s3.md#s3-faq-instant-retrieval-once-a-quarter) that still needs millisecond reads. Its objects are [immediately available using GET](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-restore-needed-flexible-deep), with no restore step. Each image is larger than [128 KB](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-glacier-ir-min-size-and-duration), so the minimum billable size does not change the cost.
takeaway: Read about once a quarter, but in milliseconds: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.
twin: If the stem said "Doctors open a given image about once a month" instead: S3 Standard-IA, because Glacier Instant Retrieval has [lower storage costs but higher data access costs](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-glacier-ir-vs-standard-ia).
say: Doctors need each image at once but rarely, so Glacier Instant Retrieval fits best.

stem: A company stores build artifacts in an Amazon S3 bucket that has S3 Versioning turned on. The number of current objects stays about the same each month, but the storage bill grows every month. Most of the stored bytes belong to noncurrent object versions. S3 Storage Lens also shows that the bucket has no lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads. The company needs every current version and wants to keep old versions for 30 days. Which combination of steps is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
keywords: no lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads

options.text: Add a lifecycle rule with the NoncurrentVersionExpiration action that permanently deletes object versions 30 days after they become noncurrent.
options.why: This action can [permanently delete noncurrent versions of objects](../facts/s3.md#s3-lifecycle-noncurrent-version-expiration), and the current versions stay untouched.

options.text: Add a lifecycle rule with an Expiration action for current object versions, so that S3 also removes the parts of incomplete multipart uploads.
options.why: Expiration actions [don't remove incomplete multipart uploads](../facts/s3.md#s3-lifecycle-expiration-keeps-incomplete-mpu), and expiring current versions hides objects that the company needs.
options.misconception: believes that an Expiration action also cleans up incomplete multipart uploads

options.text: Suspend S3 Versioning on the bucket, so that S3 removes the noncurrent object versions that the bucket already stores.
options.why: When versioning is suspended, [existing objects in your bucket do not change](../facts/s3.md#s3-versioning-suspend-keeps-existing-versions), so the old versions keep their storage cost.
options.misconception: believes that suspending versioning deletes the versions that already exist

options.text: Add a lifecycle rule that moves noncurrent object versions to S3 Glacier Deep Archive 30 days after they become noncurrent.
options.why: It works, but each archived version is billed for at least [180 days](../facts/s3.md#s3-archive-min-duration), and the company does not need versions after 30 days.

options.text: Add a lifecycle rule with the AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload action that stops uploads that are not complete 7 days after they start.
options.why: This action [stops the multipart upload and deletes the parts](../facts/s3.md#s3-lifecycle-abort-incomplete-multipart), so the bytes of unfinished uploads stop growing.

explanation: Two things grow. Normal S3 rates [apply for every version of an object](../facts/s3.md#s3-versioning-every-version-billed), so old versions cost money until a rule deletes them. The parts of unfinished uploads also stay stored until the abort action removes them, and [no objects are deleted by this lifecycle action](../facts/s3.md#s3-lifecycle-abort-incomplete-multipart).
takeaway: A versioned bucket that keeps growing: expire noncurrent versions and abort incomplete multipart uploads.
twin: If the stem said "must keep old versions for 7 years for audits" instead: move noncurrent versions to S3 Glacier Deep Archive, which is [the lowest cost storage in the cloud](../facts/s3.md#s3-class-deep-archive-lowest-cost-twelve-hours).
